steps.scene: Very heavy rain. Spray is coming off the vehicles ahead and you're holding your usual dry-road gap.

question.prompt: What has happened to your overall stopping distance?

options.text: It's much the same — a gap is a gap
It's shorter, because you're driving more slowly

question.explanation: Wet roads at least double stopping distances. Double your separation distance to match.

a.label: Wet road
a.body: Grip is reduced: your overall stopping distance roughly doubles.

b.label: Icy road
b.body: Grip nearly disappears: stopping distances can be up to TEN times greater.

question.prompt: By how much can icy conditions increase stopping distances?

options.text: About twice, the same as rain

question.explanation: Bad weather doesn't add a bit. Wet doubles it; ice can multiply it by ten.

steps.title: How a stop is built
steps.prompt: Put an emergency stop in order, from the moment the hazard appears.

items.text: The hazard appears ahead of you
Thinking distance — you travel on while you react
Braking distance — the brakes bring you down
Stopped, at the end of your overall stopping distance

steps.explanation: Overall stopping distance = thinking + braking. Weather stretches the braking part hardest.

steps.title: Ten times the gap
steps.body: On an icy road, leave up to ten times your normal following distance — and only travel at all if the journey is essential.

question.prompt: How far behind the car in front should you drive on an icy road?

options.text: A bit more than usual — say twice the gap

question.explanation: Ice is the one condition where a small increase is nowhere near enough — ten times the normal gap.

steps.title: Four small patches
steps.body: Your tyres are the only thing touching the road. Their tread and pressure change how far you need to stop.

question.prompt: Two identical cars brake hard from the same speed. What could make one stop much later?

options.text: A lower speed limit on that road
Nothing, if both sets of tyres are legal

question.explanation: Correctly inflated tyres in good condition grip best — and grip is what braking distance is made of.

steps.scene: You're moving briskly along a soaking wet road when the steering suddenly goes feather-light in your hands.

options.text: The car is handling well on the wet surface
The tyres have lifted onto the water — ease off

question.explanation: That's aquaplaning: the tyres are floating on water. Ease off and don't brake until the steering feels normal.

steps.scene: Wet road. You've left a proper gap — and a driver overtakes you and drops straight into it.

options.text: Close the gap back up to keep your place
Ease back until the gap is safe again
Flash your headlights to warn them

question.explanation: You've lost your stopping distance, not your place in a queue. Ease off until you've rebuilt it.
